waterSolubility: Low as Pb²⁺ carbonate; highly soluble as Pb(NO₃)₂ ~560 g/L
environmentalPersistence: Extremely high — does not degrade; persists indefinitely in soil

morphologicalEffects.heightSuppression: Strong — root architecture destroyed reduces nutrient/water supply to shoot
morphologicalEffects.wilting: Strong — root damage severely impairs water uptake
morphologicalEffects.chlorosis: Strong — Pb inhibits δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD), blocking heme/chlorophyll synthesis
morphologicalEffects.necrosis: Strong — root tip necrosis; dark spots on older leaves
morphologicalEffects.rootGrowth: Severely inhibited — primary toxicity site; roots turn brown-black
morphologicalEffects.newVsOldLeaves: Older leaves show chlorosis/spotting first; young leaves stunted

physiologyEffects.chlorophyllReduction: Strong — ALAD inhibition blocks chlorophyll biosynthesis directly
physiologyEffects.nutrientTransport: Strongly disrupted — Pb competes with Ca²⁺ and K⁺

temporalDynamics.recoveryTime: None — Pb is not metabolized; permanent accumulation

visualSimulation.colorChanges: Green → yellow (chlorosis); dark brown-black spots; roots turn dark
visualSimulation.damagePattern: Patchy dark spots on chlorotic background
visualSimulation.heatmapGlow: Strong dark amber glow in roots and vascular tissue — phytochelatin and δ-ALA signature
visualSimulation.microbiomeParticles: Sparse; high pathogen fraction; resistome particles increase

synergies.synergyNote: Lead + cadmium is an especially common co-contamination in industrial soils — shared phytochelatin competition mechanism; combined exposure overwhelms detox capacity
synergies.antagonismNote: Phosphate precipitates Pb²⁺ as insoluble lead phosphate, reducing bioavailability; Ca²⁺ competes at uptake sites

educationalContext.realWorldSources: Lead paint (pre-1978 buildings), leaded gasoline legacy contamination, industrial smelting, car batteries, contaminated soil near highways
educationalContext.agriculturalUse: None — legacy contaminant in urban soils and near roadsides
educationalContext.humanToxicity: Extremely high — neurotoxin especially in children; no safe exposure level; causes IQ reduction, behavioral problems, organ damage
educationalContext.climateLink: Increased flooding events mobilize lead from contaminated soils into agricultural areas
educationalContext.indoorOutdoor: Both — lead paint dust indoors; soil contamination outdoors
educationalContext.whyStudentsCare: Lead paint in older school buildings and homes — directly personal. The IQ/neurotoxicity angle is one of the most compelling environmental justice stories in science.
educationalContext.realWorldIssue: Environmental justice, urban soil contamination, childhood neurotoxicity, Flint Michigan water crisis connection
